title: I Have Been A Funeral Director For Twenty-Three Years And When An Eighty-Eight Year Old Korean War Veteran Named Earl Died Alone With Nobody To Claim Him, I Posted A Short Message Asking Strangers To Come To His Burial, And On Friday Mornin
excerpt: I have been a funeral director for twenty-three years. I grew up in this business. My father ran the funeral home before me, and his father before him. author: admin

blocks.text: PART 1 — THE CALL

I have been a funeral director for twenty-three years. I grew up in this business. My father ran the funeral home before me, and his father before him. I have helped thousands of families say goodbye. I know what grief sounds like in a quiet room. I know how to fold a flag. I know which hymns make people cry and which ones help them stop.
But the hardest calls are not the ones with grieving families. The hardest calls are the ones with no family at all.

In October, the county medical examiner called. A man had died alone in a small apartment on the east side of town. A neighbor noticed the mail piling up. He was eighty-eight years old. He had died peacefully, they believed, in his sleep, in his armchair with a radio still playing.

The medical examiner’s office searched for next of kin, the way they always do. They found no wife, no children, no siblings still living. His lease listed no emergency contact. His doctor’s office had only his own number. No one had called the apartment in months, as far as anyone could tell.

When that happens, the county has a fund for a simple burial, and our funeral home has a contract to help. It is not glamorous work. It is a plain casket, a few forms, and a quiet graveside. I have done it dozens of times. I always try to do it with care, because every person deserves care at the end. But I am honest enough to say that most of the time, it is just me, a pastor, and the cemetery staff.
The hardest calls are not the ones with grieving families. The hardest calls are the ones with no family at all.

I drove to the medical examiner’s office to bring Earl back to our funeral home. They handed me a bag with his personal effects. A watch. A pair of reading glasses. A set of keys. And a worn brown leather wallet.
PART 2 — THE CARD IN THE WALLET

I always go through the personal effects carefully. Sometimes there is a clue. A name. A photograph. A church bulletin. Something that tells me who a person was, so I can say a few true words at the grave.
Earl’s wallet had eleven dollars in it, a library card, a bus pass, and a grocery store receipt for soup, bread, and bananas.
And behind his driver’s license, there was a faded card. It was soft from being carried for decades, the corners rounded, the print almost gone. I held it under the lamp at my desk to read it.
It was a veteran’s identification card. His full name, his rank, his service number. Corporal.

That changed everything. When a veteran dies with nobody to claim him, he still has the right to be buried with honors in a national cemetery. The country owes him that. There is a process. The funeral home verifies the service records with the Department of Veterans Affairs. The VA provides the burial plot, the headstone, and the flag. And the military provides an honor guard to fold that flag and play taps.
I called the national cemetery about ninety minutes from here. They confirmed his records within two days. Corporal Earl, United States Army, served 1950 to 1952. Honorably discharged. A Bronze Star.
A Bronze Star. And he died alone in an armchair, with eleven dollars and a bus pass.

I sat at my desk for a long time that evening after everyone had gone home. I kept thinking about the soup and the bananas on that receipt. I kept thinking about how many years he must have gone to that grocery store, and how many people must have passed him in the aisles, and how none of them knew.
Nobody should be buried alone. I have believed that my entire career. I decided I was not going to let it happen to Earl.
PART 3 — THE POST

Here is the truth about unclaimed veteran funerals. Most of the time, even with full honors, nobody comes. The honor guard comes, because they always come. A chaplain comes. I come. Sometimes a cemetery employee stands at a respectful distance. That is it.

The honor guard folds the flag, and there is no one to hand it to. They give it to me, or to the chaplain. I have a shelf in my office with six folded flags on it, from six veterans who had no one. I keep them because I do not know what else to do.
I did not want Earl to be flag number seven.

Some funeral homes and veterans groups across the country have started asking the public to come to these services. I had read about it. I had never tried it myself. I was afraid nobody would show up and it would feel even worse.
But on a Tuesday night, I sat down and wrote a short message on our funeral home’s Facebook page. I kept it simple. I did not use a photo, because we did not have one of him.
“Korean War veteran Earl will be laid to rest on Friday at 11 a.m. at the national cemetery. He has no family. Nobody should be buried alone. If you can, please come.”
I added the cemetery’s address and the time. I posted it. Then I went home and had dinner with my wife and tried not to think about it.
When I checked my phone before bed, the post had been shared four hundred times.
When I woke up in the morning, it had been shared twenty-one thousand times.
“Korean War veteran Earl will be laid to rest on Friday at 11 a.m. He has no family. Nobody should be buried alone. If you can, please come.”
PART 4 — THE CALLS

The first call that Wednesday morning was from a high school band director. He asked if his students could play. Then the local American Legion called. Then the Veterans of Foreign Wars post. Then a motorcycle group that escorts veterans’ funerals. Then a woman who said she was a retired nurse and just wanted to bring flowers.
The cemetery called me at noon. The director sounded a little worried. She said they had gotten more than a hundred phone calls asking about the service. She asked how many people I expected.
We moved the service to a larger shelter at the cemetery. We added parking staff. The cemetery director arranged for a sheriff’s deputy to help with traffic.

By Thursday night, the post had been shared more than ninety thousand times. Strangers left comments from all over the country. “Thank you for your service, Earl.” “My dad was in Korea. I’ll be there for him.” “I live three states away and I can’t come, but I’m lighting a candle at eleven.”
Then, late on Thursday, I got a message that was different from the others.

It was from a man named Daniel. He said he was seventy-four years old and lived in another state. He said he had seen the post because his granddaughter showed it to him. He said he believed he knew Earl. Not personally. But he believed he knew his name.
He said his father had served in Korea. He said his father had told him, many times over the years, about a corporal named Earl who had saved his life in the winter of 1951.
“I don’t know if it’s the same man,” he wrote. “But I’m getting in my car tonight. I’ll be there at eleven.”
“I don’t know if it’s the same man. But I’m getting in my car tonight. I’ll be there at eleven.”
He did not ask me anything else. He just said he was coming.
PART 5 — TWO MILES

On Friday morning I got up at five. I polished my shoes. I put on my best black suit, the one I wear for the most important services. I drove to the funeral home and checked Earl’s casket one last time. He was dressed in a new suit we had donated. We had pinned a small American flag on the lapel.

At nine, I drove the hearse out of our parking lot toward the national cemetery. The motorcycle group was waiting at the edge of town. Twenty-two riders, all veterans or the children of veterans. They lined up in front of me and behind me, and we drove ninety minutes on the highway together.

Along the way, I started to notice things. A fire truck parked on an overpass with its ladder raised and a flag hanging from it. People standing by the side of the road with their hands over their hearts. A farmer on his tractor at the edge of a field, hat off.
When we turned onto the long road that leads to the cemetery entrance, I had to slow down.
There was a line of cars two miles long.

They were parked along both shoulders, as far as I could see. People were walking toward the cemetery from their cars. Families with kids. Old men in veterans’ caps. Teenagers in letterman jackets. Women carrying flowers. A Boy Scout troop in uniform.
My hands were shaking on the steering wheel. In twenty-three years I had never seen anything like it. I had to pull over for a minute before the gate, because I could not see through my own tears.
In twenty-three years I had never seen anything like it. I had to pull over for a minute, because I could not see through my own tears.
The cemetery staff later estimated more than two thousand people came to bury a man who died with no one.
PART 6 — THE MAN WITH THE PHOTOGRAPH
When I parked the hearse near the shelter, the crowd went silent. Two thousand people, and you could hear the wind in the trees.

The honor guard stepped forward, six soldiers in dress uniform. They carried Earl’s casket from the hearse to the shelter with slow, perfect steps. The high school band played a hymn, a little out of tune and absolutely beautiful.

And standing at the very front of the crowd, right next to the shelter, was a man in his seventies. He wore a tan windbreaker and a veteran’s cap from a different war. He was holding something in both hands, close to his chest.
He said, “I’m Daniel. I drove six hundred miles.” He had driven all night, stopping only for gas and coffee. His eyes were red. He looked exhausted and completely determined.

He handed me the photograph. It was small, black and white, with a white scalloped border. Four young soldiers in heavy winter coats, standing in the snow in front of a tent. Their breath was visible in the cold. Three of them were smiling. One of them, on the end, was not smiling, but he had his arm around the shoulders of the man next to him.

On the back, in faded ink, someone had written names. The man in the middle was Daniel’s father. And the man on the end, the one with his arm around him, was labeled: “Cpl. Earl. The one who carried me.”
I compared it to the service record in my folder. The unit matched. The year matched.
